title: Introduction to Arrays
objectives: Explain what arrays are and why they matter.
Identify problems with creating separate variables.
Describe array indexing and zero-based positioning.
theory: An array is a collection of values all of the same type stored in a single variable. Without arrays, storing ten scores would require ten separate variables: score1, score2, ..., score10. This is tedious and hard to manage.
With an array, you store all ten scores in one variable: int[] scores = new int[10]; Each score has a position in the array.
C# uses zero-based indexing. The first element is at index 0, the second at index 1, and so on. An array of 10 elements has indices 0 through 9. This is universal across programming languages.

Arrays are especially useful when processing groups of related data. Game inventories, enemy lists, high scores, and player statistics all use arrays. Professional programs rely on arrays and collections.
Arrays are fixed size. Once you declare int[] scores = new int[10];, the array always holds 10 elements. If you need a flexible size, you can use a List instead, which you will learn in Lesson 6.
terms: A collection of values of the same type.
The position of an element in an array.
tryIt: Create an array of five numbers and print each one using its index.
challenge: Create an array of animal names and print them all using a loop.
mistakes: Arrays are fixed size once created.
All elements must be the same type.
summary: Arrays store multiple values of the same type in one variable. Zero-based indexing positions elements. Arrays are essential for managing groups of data.
quiz: A collection of values of same type
